title: Transforming First-Order Linear ODEs Using Integrating Factors

canonical.:question/problem:
Consider the following first-order linear ODE for the function $y = y(x)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + 2y = 2e^{-2x}
$$

Write the equation in the form $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(y I(x) \right) = I(x)Q(x),$ where $I(x)$ is an integrating factor.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x)
$$

with $P(x) = 2$ and $Q(x) = 2e^{-2x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 2\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x) = e^{2x}$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{2x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2y) & ={e}^{2x}\cdot 2{e}^{-2x} \\ {e}^{2x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+2{e}^{2x}\cdot y & ={e}^{2x}\cdot 2{e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(y I(x)\right){:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{2x}) & ={e}^{2x}\cdot 2{e}^{-2x}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical.:question/problem:
Find the general solution of the following differential equation using the method of integrating factors.

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac {3} {x} y = \dfrac{\cos x}{x^2}, \qquad x \gt 0.
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x)
$$

with $P(x) = \dfrac{3}{x}$ and $Q(x) = \dfrac{\cos x}{x^2}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (3/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})} \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x) = x^3$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}y) & ={x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}\cdot y & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(y\cdot I(x)\right)$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{3}) & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{3})\text{d}x & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts. 

$$
\int uv'\,\textrm d x = uv - \int u' v\,\textrm d x
$$

Let $u = x, u' = 1, v' = \cos x,$ and $v = \sin x.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{x}^{3} & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ y & =\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical.:question/problem:
Solve the following initial value problem using the method of integrating factors.

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + 3x^2y = 9x^2, \qquad y(0) = 1
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
This equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x),
$$

with $P(x) = 3x^2$ and $Q(x) = 9x^2.$

We compute an integrating factor using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int 3{x}^{2}\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the equation in standard form by $I(x) = e^{x^3}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}y) & ={e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot 9{x}^{2} \\ {e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\cdot y & =9{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{3}}) & =9{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x,$ making use of the substitution $u = x^3{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{e}^{{x}^{3}})\text{d}x & =\int 9{x}^{2}{e}^{{x}^{3}}\,\text{d}x \\ y{e}^{{x}^{3}} & =\int 3{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\ y{e}^{{x}^{3}} & =3{e}^{u}+C \\ y{e}^{{x}^{3}} & =3{e}^{{x}^{3}}+C \\ y & =3+C{e}^{-{x}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

This is the general solution. To find the value of $C$ corresponding to the specific solution, we apply the initial condition $y(0) = 1$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(0) & =3+C{e}^{-{0}^{3}} \\ 1 & =3+C \\ C & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y = 3 - 2e^{-x^3}.
$$

$$

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac {3} {x} y = \dfrac{\cos x}{x^2}, \qquad x \gt 0.
$$

This equation is in the standard form

$$

with $P(x) = \dfrac{3}{x}$ and $Q(x) = \dfrac{\cos x}{x^2}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (3/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{3})} \\  & ={x}^{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we multiply our differential equation through by $I(x) = x^3$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\frac{3}{x}y) & ={x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{2}} \\ {x}^{3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+3{x}^{2}\cdot y & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we rewrite the left hand side as $\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(y\cdot I(x)\right)$ and carry out the integration:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{3}) & =x\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(y{x}^{3})\text{d}x & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

To solve this integral, we integrate by parts. 

$$
\int uv'\,\textrm d x = uv - \int u' v\,\textrm d x
$$

Let $u = x, u' = 1, v' = \cos x,$ and $v = \sin x.$ Then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}y{x}^{3} & =\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ y{x}^{3} & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x+C \\ y & =\frac{x\operatorname{sin}⁡x+\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{C}{{x}^{3}}.\end{aligned}

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)y = Q(x)
$$

with $P(x) = 2$ and $Q(x) = 2e^{-2x}.$ We proceed to find an integrating factor $I(x)$ using the definition:

$$

$$

canonical.:question/problem: For the function  $g(x,y,z) = 2 (x + 1)e^z+ yz,$  evaluate  $\dfrac{\partial g}{\partial z}$ at $(1,1,1).$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $z,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(2(x+1){e}^{z}+yz) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(2(x+1){e}^{z})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(yz) \\  & =2(x+1)\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{z})+\frac{∂}{∂z}(yz) \\  & =2(x+1){e}^{z}+y\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(1,1,1)\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂z}{|}_{(1,1,1)} & =2(1+1){e}^{1}+1 \\  & =4e+1\end{aligned}
$$

canonical.:question/problem: Find $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ for $f(x,y) =x^2y\ln{x}.$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

$$

$$

Then, we use the product rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡x) & =y\cdot (\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & =y\cdot ((2x)\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡x+{x}^{2}\cdot \left(\frac{1}{x}\right)) \\  & =y(2x\operatorname{ln}⁡x+x) \\  & =xy(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x+1)\end{aligned}
$$

$$

Then, we use the product, the chain, and the constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂y}(y{e}^{xy})-{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}) & =(\frac{∂}{∂y}(y)\cdot {e}^{xy}+y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{xy}))-{x}^{2}\cdot (2y) \\  & =(1\cdot {e}^{xy}+y\cdot {e}^{xy}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(xy))-2{x}^{2}y \\  & =({e}^{xy}+y\cdot {e}^{xy}\cdot x\cdot \frac{∂}{∂y}(y))-2{x}^{2}y \\  & =({e}^{xy}+y\cdot {e}^{xy}\cdot x\cdot 1)-2{x}^{2}y \\  & ={e}^{xy}+xy{e}^{xy}-2{x}^{2}y\end{aligned}
$$

canonical.:question/problem: For the function $f(x,y) = \dfrac{4x-y}{x+y^2},$ evaluate $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x}$ at the point $(2,-1).$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{4x-y}{x+{y}^{2}}\right) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-y)\cdot (x+{y}^{2})-(4x-y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{y}^{2})}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot (x+{y}^{2})-(4x-y)\cdot 1}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4x+4{y}^{2}-4x+y}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4{y}^{2}+y}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,-1)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(2,-1)} & =\frac{4(-1)^{2}+(-1)}{{(2+{(-1)}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4-1}{{3}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants. 

First, we use the quotient rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(\frac{4x-y}{x+{y}^{2}}\right) & =\frac{\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-y)\cdot (x+{y}^{2})-(4x-y)\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(x+{y}^{2})}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4\cdot (x+{y}^{2})-(4x-y)\cdot 1}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4x+4{y}^{2}-4x+y}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4{y}^{2}+y}{{(x+{y}^{2})}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

 

Then, we evaluate the partial derivative at the point $(2,-1)\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}{|}_{(2,-1)} & =\frac{4(-1)^{2}+(-1)}{{(2+{(-1)}^{2})}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{4-1}{{3}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\end{aligned}

canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We differentiate the given function with respect to $x,$ treating all other variables as constants.

$$

 

Now, we use the sum and constant multiple rules:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}}\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(y-{x}^{2}) & =\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}}\cdot (y\cdot \frac{∂}{∂x}(1)-\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2})) \\  & =\frac{1}{y-{x}^{2}}\cdot (y\cdot 0-2x) \\  & =-\frac{2x}{y-{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}

$$

canonical.:question/worked-solution:
The partial derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ is given by the limit 

$$
\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \lim_{h \to 0} \left(\dfrac{f(x+h,y)-f(x,y)}{h}\right).
$$

Since $f(x) = y^2 \ln{x},$  we have that 

$$
f(x+h,y) = y^2\ln(x+h).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\displaystyle \dfrac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \lim_{h \to 0}\left( \dfrac{y^2\ln(x+h) -y^2\ln{x} }{h}\right).
$$

q.:question/problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation
$x^{2}\frac{dy}{dx} = y^{4} - xy$.

title: Solving a Bernoulli Differential Equation

canonical.:question/problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{y}{x}  = \dfrac{x^2}{y} .
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + p(x)y= q(x)y^n.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}, \qquad q(x) = x^2, \qquad n=-1.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by $y^{-1},$ and we get

$$
y \dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + \dfrac{y^{2}}{x}= x^2.
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z= y^{1-n} =  y^{2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 2y \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{1}{x}z  = x^2
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{2}{x} z
		=2x^2
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)z = Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=2{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x^2$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (2{x}^{2}) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =2{x}^{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{x}^{2}) & =2{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\ z{x}^{2} & =\frac{2{x}^{5}}{5}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{2{x}^{5}+C}{5{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=5C_1.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z=y^{2}.$ This results in the general solution

$$

Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{y}{x}  = \dfrac{x^2}{y} .
$$
nearby.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + p(x)y= q(x)y^n.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x) = \dfrac{1}{x}, \qquad q(x) = x^2, \qquad n=-1.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by $y^{-1},$ and we get

$$
y \dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + \dfrac{y^{2}}{x}= x^2.
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z= y^{1-n} =  y^{2}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}  = 2y \,\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
y\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{1}{2}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}\,\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{1}{x}z  = x^2
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + \dfrac{2}{x} z
		=2x^2
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\textrm{d}z}{\textrm{d}x} + P(x)z = Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=\frac{2}{x},\,Q(x)=2{x}^{2}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (2/x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)=x^2$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+\frac{2}{x}z) & ={x}^{2}\cdot (2{x}^{2}) \\ {x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+2xz & =2{x}^{4} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{x}^{2}) & =2{x}^{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x$ and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{x}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int 2{x}^{4}\,\text{d}x \\ z{x}^{2} & =\frac{2{x}^{5}}{5}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{2{x}^{5}+C}{5{x}^{2}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=5C_1.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z=y^{2}.$ This results in the general solution

$$
y^{ 2} =\dfrac{2x^5 + C}{5x^2}.
$$

nearby.:question/problem:
Find the general solution to the differential equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-y={y}^{2}{e}^{x}.
$$
nearby.:question/worked-solution:
Notice that our equation is an instance of the Bernoulli differential equation

$$
\frac{dy}{dx}+p(x)y=q(x){y}^{n}.
$$

In this case, we have

$$
p(x)=-1,\,q(x)={e}^{x},\,n=2.
$$

First, we divide the differential equation by ${y}^{2},$ and we get

$$
{y}^{-2}\frac{dy}{dx}-{y}^{-1}={e}^{x}.\,\,(∗)
$$

Then, we make the substitution

$$
z={y}^{1-n}={y}^{-1}.
$$

Differentiating $z(x)$ using the chain rule, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}=-{y}^{-2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,⟹\,{y}^{-2}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}.
$$

 

Therefore, the original equation can be written in terms of $z(x)$ as follows:

$$
-\,\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}-z={e}^{x}
$$

This differential equation is linear, so we can use the method of integrating factors. But first, we write the above equation in standard form:

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z=-{e}^{x}
$$

The above equation is in the standard form

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+P(x)z=Q(x)
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}P(x)=1,\,Q(x)=-{e}^{x}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

We then compute an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int P(x)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\int (1)\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the standard form equation by $I(x)={e}^{x}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x}\cdot (\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z) & ={e}^{x}\cdot (-{e}^{x}) \\ {e}^{x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}x}+z{e}^{x} & =-{e}^{2x} \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{x}) & =-{e}^{2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(z{e}^{x})\,\text{d}x & =-\int {e}^{2x}\,\text{d}x \\ z{e}^{x} & =-\frac{1}{2}{e}^{2x}+{C}_{1} \\ z & =\frac{C-{e}^{2x}}{2{e}^{x}},\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2{C}_{1}.$

Finally, we determine $y(x)$ by writing $z={y}^{-1}.$ This results in

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{-1}=\frac{C-{e}^{2x}}{2{e}^{x}}\,⇒\,y=\frac{2{e}^{x}}{C-{e}^{2x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical.:question/problem:
Which of the following equations is a Bernoulli differential equation?

- $y\,y' + x^2y^2 = e^x y^4$

- $xy' + x^3y = -x^2 y^3$

- $y' + y\cos{x} = e^{y+1}$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
A Bernoulli differential equation has the form

$$
\dfrac{{{\rm{d}}y}}{{{\rm{d}}x}} + p(x)y= q(x)y^n,
$$

where $n$ is a real number.

With that in mind, let's examine the given options.

- Equation I is a Bernoulli differential equation. Writing the equation in standard form, we get

$$
y' + x^2y = e^x y^3
$$

which is a Bernoulli differential equation with

$$
p(x) = x^2, \qquad q(x) = e^x, \qquad n=3.
$$

- Equation II is a Bernoulli differential equation. Writing the equation in standard form, we get

$$
y' + x^2y = -xy^3
$$

which is a Bernoulli differential equation with

$$
p(x) = x^2, \qquad q(x) =-x, \qquad n=3.
$$

- Equation III is *not* a Bernoulli differential equation. It is missing the $q(x)y^n$ term.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

canonical.:question/problem: Given that $3\cdot 6^{x} = 9,$ find the value of $x$ rounded to $3$ decimal places.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
First, we isolate the exponential on the left-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\cdot {6}^{x} & =9 \\ {6}^{x} & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we take $\log_{6}$ of both sides of the equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}
   	6^x 					&= 3 \\[3pt]
	\log_6 \left(6^x\right)	&= \log_6 (3) \\[3pt]
	x 					&= \log_6 (3)\\[3pt]
\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we rewrite the right-hand side using the change of base formula:

$$
x = \dfrac{\log(3)}{\log(6)}
$$

Evaluating the above on a calculator gives

$$
x \approx 0.613
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

canonical.:question/problem: Given that $3^{2x+3}=5,$ find the value of $x$ rounded to $3$ decimal places.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
Taking $\log_3$ of both sides of the equation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
   	3^{2x+3} 				&= 5 \\[3pt]
	\log_3 \left(3^{2x+3}\right)	&= \log_3 (5) \\[3pt]
	2x+3 					&= \log_3 (5) . \\[3pt]
\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we rewrite the right-hand side using the change of base formula and solve for $x\mathbin{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}2x+3 & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)} \\ 2x & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}-3 \\ x & =\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(5)}{2\operatorname{log}⁡(3)}-\frac{3}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating the above expression using a calculator gives

$$
x \approx -0.768
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

**Note:** We used the change of base formula to rewrite the right-hand side, as many calculators can only compute base $10$ logarithms.

$$
y_p' = 3\alpha e ^{3x}.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}(3\alpha {e}^{3x})-2(\alpha {e}^{3x}) & =4{e}^{3x} \\ (3-2)\alpha {e}^{3x} & =4{e}^{3x} \\ \alpha {e}^{3x} & =4{e}^{3x} \\ \alpha  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
y_p(x) = 4e^{3x}.

title: Finding an Integrating Factor for an Inexact Equation: Condition on X Satisfied

canonical.:question/problem:
Find an integrating factor for the following equation in differential form.

$$
x\,y' = 4y - 3x
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y) \,\textrm{d} x+Q(x,y)\,\textrm{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
\dfrac{1}{Q} \left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right) = g(x)
$$

where $g(x)$ is independent of $y,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(x) = \exp\left({\int g(x)\,\textrm d x}\right)
$$

where $\exp(x)$ denotes the exponential function $e^x.$

First, we rewrite our equation in differential form: 

$$
(3x - 4y) \;\textrm{d}x  + (x) \;\textrm{d} y  =0
$$

Let's denote 

$$
P(x,y) = 3x - 4y, \qquad Q(x,y) = x.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x-4y)=-4 \\ \frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x}) & =\frac{1}{x}(-4-1) \\  & =-\frac{5}{x},\end{aligned}
$$

is a function of $x$ only, we can conclude that an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(\int -\frac{5}{x}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(-5\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|) \\  & ={x}^{-5}\end{aligned}
$$

and by multiplying our differential equation by the integrating factor, we have

$$
I(x) \cdot \left((3x - 4y) \;\textrm{d}x + x\;\textrm{d} y\right) =  I(x)\cdot 0
$$

which simplifies as

$$
x^{-5} \cdot \left((3x - 4y) \;\textrm{d}x + x\;\textrm{d} y\right) = 0.
$$

I(x)=\operatorname{exp}⁡(\int g(x)\,\text{d}x)

$$
\frac{1}{Q}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x})=\frac{3}{x}.
$$

Since $\frac{3}{x}$ is a function of $x$ only, we can conclude that the integrating factor for the equation is 

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int 3{x}^{-1}\text{ }\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{3\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={x}^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}[(\frac{6{y}^{2}}{x}+4{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x+(4y+3x{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})\,\text{d}y] & =0 \\ \underbrace{(6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{x}^{3}{y}^{3})}_{\overset{~}{P}}\,\text{d}x+\underbrace{(4{x}^{3}y+3{x}^{4}{y}^{2}+1)}_{\overset{~}{Q}}\,\text{d}y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

For this exact equation, we have

$$
\overset{~}{P}(x,y)=6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{x}^{3}{y}^{3},\,\overset{~}{Q}(x,y)=4{x}^{3}y+3{x}^{4}{y}^{2}+1.
$$

The result should include an arbitrary function of $y,$ which we'll call $F(y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{P}(x,y)\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\int (6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{x}^{3}{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{x}^{4}{y}^{3}+F(y).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's integrate $\overset{~}{Q}(x,y)$ with respect to $y.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $x,$ which we'll call $G(x):$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{Q}(x,y)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\int (4{x}^{3}y+3{x}^{4}{y}^{2}+1)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =2{x}^{3}{y}^{2}+{x}^{4}{y}^{3}+y+G(x).\end{aligned}

canonical.:question/problem:
Consider the inexact differential equation

$$
\left(x + y^2\right)\,\textrm{d}x + \left(xy + \frac{2}{x}\right)\,\textrm{d}y = 0.
$$

It is known that

$$
\dfrac{1}{Q}\left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}-\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right)=\frac{1}{x}
$$

where the functions $P$ and $Q$ are given by

$$
P(x,y)=x+y^2,\qquad Q(x,y)=xy+\frac{2}{x}.
$$

Use this information to find a suitable integrating factor $I(x)$ and hence find the general solution to the equation.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\textrm{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\textrm{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
\dfrac{1}{Q}\left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}-\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right)=g(x)
$$

where $g(x)$ is independent of $y,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(x)=\exp\left(\int g(x)\,\textrm{d}x\right)
$$

where $\exp(x)$ denotes the exponential function $e^x.$

We are given that

$$
\dfrac{1}{Q}\left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}-\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right)=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Since $\dfrac{1}{x}$ is a function of $x$ only, we can conclude that the integrating factor for the equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int {x}^{-1}\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our equation by the integrating factor, we arrive at the following exact differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x[(x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x+(xy+\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}y] & =0 \\ \underbrace{({x}^{2}+x{y}^{2})}_{\overset{~}{P}}\,\text{d}x+\underbrace{({x}^{2}y+2)}_{\overset{~}{Q}}\,\text{d}y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For this exact equation, we have

$$
\widetilde{P}(x,y)=x^2+xy^2,\qquad
\widetilde{Q}(x,y)=x^2y+2.
$$

To solve the equation, let's first integrate $\widetilde{P}(x,y)$ with respect to $x.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $y,$ which we'll call $F(y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{P}(x,y)\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\int ({x}^{2}+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{2}+F(y).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's integrate $\widetilde{Q}(x,y)$ with respect to $y.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $x,$ which we'll call $G(x){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{Q}(x,y)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\int ({x}^{2}y+2)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{2}+2y+G(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the two solutions, we must have

$$
F(y)=2y,\qquad G(x)=\frac{x^3}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution $u(x,y)=c$ is

$$
\frac{x^3}{3}+\frac{x^2y^2}{2}+2y=c.
$$

We are given that

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{3}[(\frac{6{y}^{2}}{x}+4{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x+(4y+3x{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{{x}^{3}})\,\text{d}y] & =0 \\ \underbrace{(6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4{x}^{3}{y}^{3})}_{\overset{~}{P}}\,\text{d}x+\underbrace{(4{x}^{3}y+3{x}^{4}{y}^{2}+1)}_{\overset{~}{Q}}\,\text{d}y & =0\end{aligned}

$$

$$

canonical.:question/problem:
Consider the inexact differential equation

$$
\left(x + y^2\right)\,\textrm{d}x + \left(xy + \frac{2}{x}\right)\,\textrm{d}y = 0.
$$

It is known that

$$
\dfrac{1}{Q}\left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}-\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right)=\frac{1}{x}
$$

where the functions $P$ and $Q$ are given by

$$
P(x,y)=x+y^2,\qquad Q(x,y)=xy+\frac{2}{x}.
$$

Use this information to find a suitable integrating factor $I(x)$ and hence find the general solution to the equation.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\,\textrm{d}x+Q(x,y)\,\textrm{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
\dfrac{1}{Q}\left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}-\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right)=g(x)
$$

where $g(x)$ is independent of $y,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(x)=\exp\left(\int g(x)\,\textrm{d}x\right)
$$

where $\exp(x)$ denotes the exponential function $e^x.$

We are given that

$$
\dfrac{1}{Q}\left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y}-\dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right)=\frac{1}{x}.
$$

Since $\dfrac{1}{x}$ is a function of $x$ only, we can conclude that the integrating factor for the equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & ={e}^{\int {x}^{-1}\,\text{d}x} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying our equation by the integrating factor, we arrive at the following exact differential equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}x[(x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x+(xy+\frac{2}{x})\,\text{d}y] & =0 \\ \underbrace{({x}^{2}+x{y}^{2})}_{\overset{~}{P}}\,\text{d}x+\underbrace{({x}^{2}y+2)}_{\overset{~}{Q}}\,\text{d}y & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For this exact equation, we have

$$
\widetilde{P}(x,y)=x^2+xy^2,\qquad
\widetilde{Q}(x,y)=x^2y+2.
$$

To solve the equation, let's first integrate $\widetilde{P}(x,y)$ with respect to $x.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $y,$ which we'll call $F(y){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{P}(x,y)\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\int ({x}^{2}+x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x+F(y) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{2}+F(y).\end{aligned}
$$

Next, let's integrate $\widetilde{Q}(x,y)$ with respect to $y.$
The result should include an arbitrary function of $x,$ which we'll call $G(x){:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}u(x,y) & =\int \overset{~}{Q}(x,y)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\int ({x}^{2}y+2)\,\text{d}y+G(x) \\  & =\frac{{x}^{2}{y}^{2}}{2}+2y+G(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Comparing the two solutions, we must have

$$
F(y)=2y,\qquad G(x)=\frac{x^3}{3}.
$$

Therefore, the general solution $u(x,y)=c$ is

$$
\frac{x^3}{3}+\frac{x^2y^2}{2}+2y=c.
$$

title: Testing Integrating Factors for ODEs in Differential Form

canonical.:question/problem:
Show that $I(x) = \dfrac{1}{xy^3}$ is an integrating factor of the equation 

$$
(x^2y-y^3) \,\textrm{d}x - x^{3} \,\textrm{d}y = 0
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
A function $I(x,y)$ is an integrating factor for the differential equation

$$
P(x,y) \,\textrm{d} x+Q(x,y)\,\textrm{d}y=0,
$$

if the following equation is exact:

$$
I(x,y)[P(x,y) \,\textrm{d} x+Q(x,y)\,\textrm{d}y] = 0
$$

In our case, we need to check if the following equation is exact:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{x{y}^{3}}(({x}^{2}y-{y}^{3})\,\text{d}x-{x}^{3}\,\text{d}y) & =0 \\ (\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{x})\,\text{d}x-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{3}}\,\text{d}y & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Recall that a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y)\, \textrm{d}x +Q(x,y)\, \textrm{d}y = 0
$$

is exact if it passes the exactness test, i.e.,

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial y} = \frac{\partial Q}{\partial x}.
$$

For our transformed equation, we have  

$$
P(x,y) = \dfrac{x}{y^2}-\dfrac{1}{x}, \qquad Q(x,y) =- \dfrac{x^2}{y^3}.
$$

Now, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{x}{{y}^{2}}-\frac{1}{x})=-\frac{2x}{{y}^{3}} \\ \frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}\left(-\frac{{x}^{2}}{{y}^{3}}\right)=-\frac{2x}{{y}^{3}}\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\frac{\partial P}{\partial y}=\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x},
$$

the transformed equation $\text{is}$ exact.

Therefore, $I(x)=\dfrac{1}{xy^3}$ $\text{is}$ an integrating factor for the initial differential equation.

title: Finding an Integrating Factor for an Inexact Equation: Condition on X Satisfied

canonical.:question/problem:
Find an integrating factor for the following equation in differential form.

$$
x\,y' = 4y - 3x
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y) \,\textrm{d} x+Q(x,y)\,\textrm{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
\dfrac{1}{Q} \left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right) = g(x)
$$

where $g(x)$ is independent of $y,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(x) = \exp\left({\int g(x)\,\textrm d x}\right)
$$

where $\exp(x)$ denotes the exponential function $e^x.$

First, we rewrite our equation in differential form: 

$$
(3x - 4y) \;\textrm{d}x  + (x) \;\textrm{d} y  =0
$$

Let's denote 

$$
P(x,y) = 3x - 4y, \qquad Q(x,y) = x.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3x-4y)=-4 \\ \frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}x=1\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{Q}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x}) & =\frac{1}{x}(-4-1) \\  & =-\frac{5}{x},\end{aligned}
$$

is a function of $x$ only, we can conclude that an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}I(x) & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(\int -\frac{5}{x}\,\text{d}x) \\  & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(-5\operatorname{ln}⁡|x|) \\  & ={x}^{-5}\end{aligned}
$$

and by multiplying our differential equation by the integrating factor, we have

$$
I(x) \cdot \left((3x - 4y) \;\textrm{d}x + x\;\textrm{d} y\right) =  I(x)\cdot 0
$$

which simplifies as

$$
x^{-5} \cdot \left((3x - 4y) \;\textrm{d}x + x\;\textrm{d} y\right) = 0.
$$

title: Finding an Integrating Factor for an Inexact Equation: Condition on Y Satisfied

canonical.:question/problem:
Find an integrating factor for the following differential equation.

$$
y^2 \; \textrm{d}x + xy \; \textrm{d}y = 0, \qquad y > 0
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
For a differential equation of the form

$$
P(x,y) \,\textrm{d} x+Q(x,y)\,\textrm{d}y=0,
$$

we have that if

$$
\dfrac{1}{P} \left(\dfrac{\partial P}{\partial y} - \dfrac{\partial Q}{\partial x}\right) = h(y)
$$

where $h(y)$ is independent of $x,$ then an integrating factor for the equation is

$$
I(y) = \exp\left({-\int h(y)\,\textrm d y}\right)
$$

where $\exp(y)$ denotes the exponential function $e^y.$

Let's denote

$$
P(x,y) =  y^2, \qquad Q(x,y) =  xy.
$$

Now, let's compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(xy)=y\end{aligned}
$$

Since

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{P}(\frac{∂P}{∂y}-\frac{∂Q}{∂x}) & =\frac{1}{{y}^{2}}(2y-y) \\  & ={y}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

is a function of $y$ only, we can conclude that an integrating factor for our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}I(y) & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(\int -({y}^{-1})\,\text{d}y) \\  & =\operatorname{exp}⁡(-\operatorname{ln}⁡y) \\  & ={y}^{-1}\end{aligned}
$$

and by multiplying our differential equation by the integrating factor, we have

$$
I(y)\cdot \left(y^2 \; \textrm{d}x + xy\; \textrm{d}y \right) = I(y)\cdot 0
$$

which simplifies as

$$
\bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{y^{-1}\left(y^2 \; \textrm{d}x + xy \; \textrm{d}y \right) = 0}.
$$

title: Sketching the Phase Portrait of a System

canonical.:question/problem:
Consider the system of linear differential equations below.

$$
\left\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t) &=-y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t) &=9x(t)\end{aligned}\right.
$$

The eigenvalues of the system's matrix are $\lambda_{1,2} = \pm3\text{i},$ for which the corresponding eigenvectors are $\mathbf{v}_{1,2} = [\pm \text{i}, 3]^T,$ respectively. Given that the general solution of the system is
$$
{\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( t ) \\ y ( t )\end{array} \right]} = 
c_1 {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- \sin   ( 3 t ) \\ 3 \cos   ( 3 t )\end{array} \right]} +

\qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R},
$$
sketch the phase portrait of the system of differential equations given above.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We are given that the general solution of the system is $$ {\left[ \begin{array}{c}x ( t ) \\ y ( t )\end{array} \right]} = c_1 {\left[ \begin{array}{c}- \sin ( 3 t ) \\ 3 \cos ( 3 t )\end{array} \right]} + c_2 {\left[ \begin{array}{c}\cos ( 3 t ) \\ 3 \sin ( 3 t )\end{array} \right]}, \qquad c_1,c_2 \in \mathbb{R}. $$ For example, when $c_1=1$ and $c_2=0,$ we obtain the following curve: $$ \left\{\begin{aligned}x &=-\operatorname{sin}⁡(3t) \\ y &=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(3t)\end{aligned}\right. $$ Computing the coordinates (rounded to two decimal places) of several points on the curve, we get the table below.

$x$ $0$ $-0.71$ $-1$
$y$ $3$ $2.12$ $0$

q.:question/problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $4{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2}.$ Which differential equation describes this motion?
q.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/88/888a2f1f537f7381379a6f85dc850f29b42193eb53938832be8ede47fbe8264a.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $4{x}^{2}\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=4{x}^{2}.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=4{x}^{2}.
$$

Now, since $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t},$ we obtain the differential equation

$$
v\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=4{x}^{2}.
$$

title: Finding a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle

canonical.:question/problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis where $x>0$. When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x$ meters, its velocity is $v\, \rm{ m/s}$ and the magnitude of its acceleration is $\sin^2 x \,\rm{m/s}^2.$ Given that the acceleration is directed toward $O,$ what differential equation describes this motion?
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/f1/f187eff194f136838b67ab12b44f8f6882eafb59885a5c3f440d41492def4a42.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\sin^2 x$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = -\sin^2 x.
$$

Using the chain rule for differentiation, we can rewrite this equation as

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-{sin}^{2}⁡x.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v= \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t},$ we have

$$
v \dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}x} = -\sin^2 x.\qquad \qquad (\ast)
$$

Finally, using the fact that

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}(v^2) = 2v\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac12v^2\right) = v\dfrac{\textrm d v}{\textrm d x},
$$

we can write our differential equation $(\ast)$ as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d }{\textrm d x}\left(\dfrac12v^2\right) = -\sin^2 x.
$$

q.:question/problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x\,m,$ its velocity is $v\,m/s$ and its acceleration is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2}.$ If $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x=3\,\text{m}.$ Round your answer to one decimal place.
q.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/ec/ec4af1357e75dcee6d7d5412467c2ee2ea9e54fa38fb6e83817b0ae909c529aa.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2+3{e}^{-x})\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=2+3{e}^{-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=2+3{e}^{-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int (2+3{e}^{-x})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2x-3{e}^{-x}+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\text{m/s}$ when $x=0\,\text{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =2(0)-3{e}^{-0}+C \\ 2 & =-3+C \\ C & =2+3 \\ C & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2x-3{e}^{-x}+5 \\ {v}^{2} & =4x-6{e}^{-x}+10 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{4x-6{e}^{-x}+10}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v=\sqrt{4x-6{e}^{-x}+10}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x=3$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{4(3)-6{e}^{-3}+10} \\ v & =\sqrt{22-6{e}^{-3}} \\ v & ≈4.7\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

title: Solving a Differential Equation That Relates the Velocity and Displacement of a Particle

canonical.:question/problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x,$ away from a fixed origin $O.$ When the displacement of $P$ from $O$ is $x \,\rm{m},$ its velocity is $v\,\rm{m/s}$ and its acceleration is $(2x + e^{x-2}) \, \rm{m/s}^2.$ If $v = 4 \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 2 \, \textrm m,$ find the velocity of $P$ when $x = 1 \, \textrm m.$ Round your answer to two decimal places.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/4f/4fdd70a4ca80965c0adce9c60be36b0712852b662cff69f9733f50c739fd1b32.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $(2x + e^{x-2}) \,\rm{m/s}^2,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} = 2x + e^{x-2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = 2x + e^{x-2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int (2x+{e}^{x-2})\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\dfrac{1}{2}v^2 = x^2 + e^{x-2} + C.
$$

Now, since $v = 4 \, \rm{m/s}$ when $x = 2 \, \textrm m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C$, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}(4)^{2} & ={2}^{2}+{e}^{2-2}+C \\ 8 & =4+1+C \\ C & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & ={x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3 \\ {v}^{2} & =2({x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3) \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{2({x}^{2}+{e}^{x-2}+3)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x) \gt 0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v = \sqrt{2\left(x^2 + e^{x-2} + 3\right)}.
$$

Finally, the velocity of $P$ at $x = 1$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =\sqrt{2({1}^{2}+{e}^{1-2}+3)} \\  & =\sqrt{2(4+{e}^{-1})} \\  & ≈2.96\,\text{m/s},\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to two decimal places.

$$

$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x=\int 4x\,\text{d}x

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=2{x}^{2}+C.

q.:question/problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin $O$ is $x\,\text{m},$ the magnitude of its acceleration is $2{e}^{-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed toward $O.$ Initially, $P$ is at the origin $O$ and has velocity $v=2\,m/s.$ Find $x$ as a function of time $t.$
q.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/ad/ad437638f22672a10a183f1521929637f8d43725f37a9736c569516232e7c468.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $2{e}^{-x}\,{m/s}^{2}$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=-2{e}^{-x}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=-2{e}^{-x}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -2{e}^{-x}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $x=0\,\text{m}$ when $v=2\,\text{m/s},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =2{e}^{0}+K \\ K & =2-2 \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2{e}^{-x} \\ {v}^{2} & =4{e}^{-x} \\ v & =\pm 2{e}^{-x/2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=2{e}^{-x/2}.
$$

Now, we know that $v=\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=2{e}^{-x/2}.
$$

Separating the variables and integrating both sides with respect to $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2{e}^{-x/2} \\ {e}^{x/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =2 \\ \int {e}^{x/2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ \int {e}^{x/2}\text{d}x & =\int 2\,\text{d}t \\ 2{e}^{x/2} & =2t+{C}_{1} \\ {e}^{x/2} & =t+C\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=\frac{{C}_{1}}{2}.$ 

We're given that $x=0$ when $t=0.$ Therefore, $C=1,$ and the particular solution is

$$
{e}^{x/2}=t+1.
$$

Finally, writing $x$ in terms of $t,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{x/2} & =t+1 \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{x/2}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1) \\ \frac{x}{2} & =\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1) \\ x & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡(t+1).\end{aligned}
$$

canonical.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/ec/eca36626e6a0cfb30d293e684483c37ddce6f18d4004c3f77258e9663565d8d7.png)

Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ has magnitude $\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}\, \rm{m/s}^2$ and is directed *toward* $O,$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t} =-\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Using the fact that 

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}v}{\textrm{d}t}= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right)
$$

we can rewrite our equation as

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\dfrac{1}{2}v^2\right) = -\dfrac{2}{(x+1)^2}.
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\,\text{d}x & =\int -\frac{2}{(x+1)^{2}}\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1}+K.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $v=2\,\rm{m/s}$ when $x=0\, \textrm{m},$ we can find the value of the constant $K,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1}+K \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =\frac{2}{0+1}+K \\ 2 & =2+K \\ K & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =\frac{2}{x+1} \\ {v}^{2} & =\frac{4}{x+1} \\ v & =\pm \frac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing  $x,$ we have that $v(x) > 0,$ so we can discard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x) = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

Now, we know that $v= \dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t}.$ Therefore, we have the equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}x}{\textrm{d}t} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{x+1}}.
$$

title: Identifying Solutions to Initial Value Problems

canonical.:question/problem:
Consider the following initial value problem

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x} = \dfrac{3y}{x}, \qquad y(-1) = -2.
$$

You're given that $y = Ax^3$ is the solution to this initial value problem. What is the value of the constant $A?$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We're given that $y = Ax^3$ is the solution to the initial value problem. Therefore, it must satisfy the differential equation *and* the initial condition $y(-1) = -2.$

Substituting the initial condition $y({\color{red}{-1}}) = {\color{blue}{-2}}$ into our solution and solving for $A,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =A{x}^{3} \\ -2 & =A(-1)^{3} \\ -2 & =A(-1) \\ A & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y = 2x^3 .
$$

title: Evaluating Using Direct Substitution

canonical.:question/problem:
Find $$
\displaystyle \lim_{x \to 1} (3^{2x} + 2^{3x} + 1).
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We can evaluate this limit using direct substitution, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to 1}({3}^{2x}+{2}^{3x}+1) & ={3}^{2(1)}+{2}^{3(1)}+1 \\  & =9+8+1 \\  & =18\end{aligned}
$$

canonical.:question/problem:
Compute $$
\displaystyle \lim_{x \to \infty} -5 \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{1+x}.
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We can use the laws of exponents and the algebra of limits to rewrite the given limit as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\lim_{x\to \infty }-5{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{1+x} & =-5\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{1+x} \\  & =-5\lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{1}\cdot {\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{x} \\  & =-5\lim_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{3}\cdot {\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{x} \\  & =-\frac{5}{3}\cdot \lim_{x\to \infty }{\left(\frac{1}{3}\right)}^{x}\end{aligned}
$$

![](images/81/81be7f2983aeb647a8fa88e2caad8cea3c2052190222670838077e760a2e7fda.png)

From the graph, we see that the function decreases to zero as $x$ increases. So

$$
\lim_{x \to \infty}   \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x} = 0,
$$

-\dfrac{5}{3}\cdot \lim_{x \to \infty}   \left(\dfrac{1}{3}\right)^{x} = -\dfrac 5 3\cdot 0 = 0.

$$
\lim_{x\to-\infty} \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x = \infty.
$$

$$
-3\cdot \lim_{x\to-\infty} \left(\dfrac 1 2\right)^x = -\infty.
$$

canonical.:question/problem: During an experiment, the weight $W(t)$ of an object varies according to the differential equation $W'(t) = -r W(t),$ where $t$ is the time, measured in hours, and $r > 0.$ It is known that the object's weight reduces by three-quarters after the first two hours. How long does it take for the object's weight to reduce to one-sixth of its original weight? Round your answer to one decimal place.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
The general solution to the given differential equation is

$$
W(t) = W_0 e^{-rt},
$$

where $W_0$ is the weight when $t=0.$

Let $t_1$ be the time when the weight equals $\dfrac{1}{6}W_0.$ Then, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}W({t}_{1}) & =\frac{1}{6}{W}_{0}\,⇒\,{W}_{0}{e}^{-r{t}_{1}}=\frac{1}{6}{W}_{0}.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve this equation for $t_1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{0}{e}^{-r{t}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{6}{W}_{0} \\ \cancel{{W}_{0}}{e}^{-r{t}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{6}\cancel{{W}_{0}} \\ {e}^{-r{t}_{1}} & =\frac{1}{6} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-r{t}_{1}}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{6}\right) \\ -r{t}_{1} & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡6 \\ {t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}{r}\,\,(∗)\end{aligned}
$$

We now need to calculate $r.$ We're told that the weight reduces by three-quarters after the first two hours. Therefore, one-quarter of the weight remains, and we have

$$
W(2) = \dfrac{1}{4}W_0\quad \Rightarrow\quad W_0e^{-2r} = \dfrac{1}{4}W_0
$$

We solve this equation for $r,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{W}_{0}{e}^{-2r} & =\frac{1}{4}{W}_{0} \\ \cancel{{W}_{0}}{e}^{-2r} & =\frac{1}{4}\cancel{{W}_{0}} \\ {e}^{-2r} & =\frac{1}{4} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-2r}) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡\left(\frac{1}{4}\right) \\ -2r & =-\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ r & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{ln}⁡4 \\ r & =\operatorname{ln}⁡{4}^{1/2} \\ r & =\operatorname{ln}⁡2\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting this into $(*)$ and evaluating, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}{r} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡6}{\operatorname{ln}⁡2} \\  & ≈2.6\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place. 

Therefore, we conclude that it takes approximately $2.6$ hours for the weight to reduce to one-sixth of its original weight.

canonical.:question/problem: A marathon runner is participating in a race. The remaining distance $D(t)$ they have left to run $t$ hours since starting the race can be modeled by the differential equation $D'(t)= -0.8D(t).$ Two hours into the race, they have $6\,\text{km}$ remaining. Calculate the distance remaining after four hours.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
The general solution to the given differential equation is

$$
D(t) = D_0\,e^{-0.8t},
$$

where $D_0$ is the remaining distance when $t=0.$

We are given that the remaining distance was $6\,\text{km}$ after $2$ hours. So, substituting $t=2$ and $D(2)=6$ into our general solution and solving for $D_0,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}D(2) & ={D}_{0}\,{e}^{-0.8\cdot 2} \\ 6 & ={D}_{0}\,{e}^{-1.6} \\ {D}_{0} & =\frac{6}{{e}^{-1.6}} \\  & ≈29.718,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Hence, our particular solution is

$$
D(t) = 29.718\,e^{-0.8t}.
$$

We want to find the distance remaining after $4$ hours. So, substituting $t=4$ into our particular solution, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}D(4) & =29.718\,{e}^{-0.8\cdot 4} \\  & =29.718\,{e}^{-3.2} \\  & ≈1.2,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to one decimal place.

Therefore, the remaining distance after $4$ hours is $1.2\,\text{km}.$

\begin{aligned}S(20) & ={S}_{0}\,{e}^{0.11\cdot 20} \\ 60\,000 & ={S}_{0}\,{e}^{2.2} \\ {S}_{0} & =\frac{60\,000}{{e}^{2.2}} \\  & ≈6\,648.190,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $3$ decimal places.

Hence, our particular solution is

$$
S(t)=6\,648.190\,{e}^{0.11t}.
$$

We want to find the number of subscribers after $32$ weeks. So, substituting $t=32$ into our particular solution, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}S(32) & =6\,648.190\,{e}^{0.11\cdot 32} \\  & =6\,648.190\,{e}^{3.52} \\  & ≈224\,605,\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to the nearest whole number. 

Therefore, the streaming service will have about $224\,605$ subscribers after $32$ weeks.

canonical.:question/problem:
The rate at which the balance in a savings account grows $B(t),$ after $t$ years, can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d B}{\textrm d t} = 0.05B.
$$

How many years does it take for the balance to increase by $60\%?$  Round your answer to the nearest year.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We model the balance growth using the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm d B}{\textrm d t} = 0.05B.
$$

The solution to this equation is

$$
B(t) = B_0\,e^{0.05t},
$$

where $B_0$ is the initial balance.

Let $t_1$ be the time when the balance has increased by $60\%.$ That is,

$$
B(t_1) = 1.6B_0.
$$

We solve the above equation for $t_1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}B({t}_{1}) & ={B}_{0}{e}^{0.05\cdot {t}_{1}} \\ 1.6{B}_{0} & ={B}_{0}{e}^{0.05{t}_{1}} \\ 1.6 & ={e}^{0.05{t}_{1}} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(1.6) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{0.05{t}_{1}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(1.6) & =0.05{t}_{1} \\ {t}_{1} & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(1.6)}{0.05} \\ {t}_{1} & ≈9.40\end{aligned}
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we conclude that it takes $9$ years for the balance to increase by $60\%.$

The rate at which the amount of medicine in a person’s bloodstream decreases $M(t),$ after $t$ hours, can be modeled by the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}M}{\textrm{d}t} = -0.08M.
$$

How many hours does it take for the amount of medicine to decrease to $30\%$ of the original amount?  Round your answer to the nearest hour.
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
We model the amount of medicine using the differential equation

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}M}{\textrm{d}t} = -0.08M.
$$

The solution to this equation is

$$
M(t) = M_0\,e^{-0.08t},
$$

where $M_0$ is the initial amount of medicine.

Let $t_1$ be the time when the amount of medicine is $30\%$ of the original amount. That is,

$$
M(t_1) = 0.30M_0.
$$

We solve the above equation for $t_1,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}0.30{M}_{0} & ={M}_{0}\,{e}^{-0.08{t}_{1}} \\ 0.30 & ={e}^{-0.08{t}_{1}} \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.30) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({e}^{-0.08{t}_{1}}) \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡(0.30) & =-0.08{t}_{1} \\ {t}_{1} & =-\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡(0.30)}{0.08} \\ {t}_{1} & ≈15.050\end{aligned}
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer, we conclude that it takes $15$ hours for the amount of medicine to decrease to $30\%$ of the original amount.

q.:question/problem:
Write the following first-order linear ODE in standard form.

$$
2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x=1-4y\operatorname{sin}⁡x
$$
q.:question/worked-solution:
A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+P(x)y=Q(x).
$$

Converting the given equation to standard form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-3\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =1-4y\operatorname{sin}⁡x \\ 2\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+4y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =1+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\underbrace{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}_{P(x)}y & =\underbrace{\frac{1+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}}_{Q(x)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x$ and $Q(x)=\frac{1+3\operatorname{cos}⁡x}{2}.$

A first-order linear ODE is in standard form if it is written as

$$
\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}
+
P(x)y
=
Q(x).
$$

Converting the given equation to standard form, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x-\operatorname{cos}⁡x & =0 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+y\operatorname{sin}⁡x & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}+\underbrace{(\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}_{P(x)}y & =\underbrace{\operatorname{cos}⁡x}_{Q(x)}\,.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the equation is written in standard form with $P(x)=\sin x$ and $Q(x) = \cos x.$

title: Using Integration by Parts to Compute an Indefinite Integral Containing an Exponential Expression

canonical.:question/problem:
Calculate $$
\displaystyle \int xe^{7x} \textrm{d}x.
$$
canonical.:question/worked-solution:
To solve this integral, we use the by-parts formula, given by

$$
\int uv' \, \textrm{d}x= uv - \int vu' \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

We need to express $\displaystyle  \int xe^{7x} \textrm{d}x$ as $\displaystyle  \int uv'\,\textrm{d}x.$ Therefore, we set

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,{u}^{′}=1 \\ {v}^{′}={e}^{7x}\, & ⟹\,v=\frac{1}{7}{e}^{7x}.\end{aligned}
$$

We substitute the above into the integration by parts formula, and we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int u{v}^{′}\,\text{d}x & =uv-\int v{u}^{′}\,\text{d}x \\ \int x\cdot {e}^{7x}\,\text{d}x & =x\cdot \frac{1}{7}{e}^{7x}-\int \frac{1}{7}{e}^{7x}\cdot 1\,\text{d}x\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we calculate the integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x{e}^{7x}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{7}x{e}^{7x}-\frac{1}{7}\int {e}^{7x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{7}x{e}^{7x}-\frac{1}{7}\left(\frac{{e}^{7x}}{7}\right)+C \\  & =\frac{1}{7}x{e}^{7x}-\frac{1}{49}{e}^{7x}+C\end{aligned}
$$
